subject: Copywriting
title: Brevity Is the Soul of Slogans
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Brevity Is the Soul of Slogans.

hook.text: 'Got Milk?' Two words. 'Just Do It.' Three words. 'Think Different.' Two words. The greatest slogans are the shortest.

buildup.text: Working memory holds 7 items, plus or minus 2. A slogan with 2-4 words fits easily. Longer slogans strain recall.

discovery.text: Slogans under 5 words are recalled 80% more than those over 10. Each extra word reduces memorability significantly.

twist.text: 'Because You're Worth It' is 4 words and L'Oréal's most valuable asset. Short doesn't mean shallow—it means distilled.

climax.text: The writer's challenge: compress the brand's entire promise into the fewest possible words. Distillation is the skill.

punchline.text: Two words can be worth billions. Brevity is a slogan's power.

quiz.question: How much more are slogans under 5 words recalled compared to longer ones?

details.summary: Great slogans distill complex brand promises into just a few words. Brevity forces precision, and precision creates memorability. The most enduring slogans in history rarely exceed five words, proving that less truly is more in persuasive language.
details.whyItMatters: In an age of information overload, brevity is a competitive advantage. Learning why short slogans stick helps anyone craft messages that cut through noise.
takeaways: The best slogans are typically three to five words long
Brevity forces writers to find the emotional essence of a brand
Short phrases are easier to recall and repeat

faq.question: Why are shorter slogans more effective than longer ones?
faq.answer: Short slogans exploit how memory works. The brain stores compact phrases as single units, making them easier to recall. Longer messages require more cognitive effort and are more likely to be forgotten or misquoted.

faq.question: Is there a perfect word count for a slogan?
faq.answer: Research suggests three to five words is the sweet spot, but exceptions exist. 'A Diamond Is Forever' is four words; 'Just Do It' is three. The real test is whether the phrase feels complete and effortless to say aloud.
